    #164898. Industry News: NBA MVP Rankings: Luka Dončić, Victor Wembanyama in a two-horse race; Stephen Curry's absence speaks volumes

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1540 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cbssports ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: NBA MVP Rankings: Luka Dončić, Victor Wembanyama in a two-horse race; Stephen Curry's absence speaks volumes

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1540 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We're nearly a month into the 2026-27 NBA season, and while some people say it's too early to start talking about MVP, we are not among those people.
    • According to recent reports, right now, it's a clear two-horse race: Luka Doncic or Victor Wembanyama?
    • According to recent reports, the Luka Dončić we're watching right now isn't just the best offensive player in the world.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We're nearly a month into the 2026-27 NBA season, and while some people say it's too early to start talking about MVP, we are not among those people.

    According to recent reports, right now, it's a clear two-horse race: Luka Doncic or Victor Wembanyama? There is a real split on this. Here's where I stand as of Tuesday, Nov. 17.

    According to recent reports, the Luka Dončić we're watching right now isn't just the best offensive player in the world. He might be the best in history. Nobody has ever put up anything close to the numbers he is charting at the moment: 39 points per game with seven assists, seven boards, nearly two steals and a positively scorching 66.0 TS%, the latter being a number even the great Stephen Curry has only bested twice in his career.

    It's early, sure. Dončić isn't likely to keep making 3s at this rate for an entire season, and indeed we've seen some slippage of late (35% over his last four, if you really want to split hairs), but his volume remains, with 4.5 makes a night over that stretch. Dončić remains on track to break Curry's single-season record of 402 3-pointers, and he's done more off-ball shooting than in the past.

    Industry observers note that throw in more transition production and a 53% midrange conversion rate, per Cleaning The Glass, and you're seeing a more diverse scorer, which is to say this isn't just a guy who has started off hot on his step-back 3s (though this is a major factor, too, of course), but a guy piercing defenses from more spots with different shots. If Dončić could actually be any harder to guard than he has been in the past, we're seeing it this season.

    He's also defending. His 23 steals rank sixth league-wide. Only two players have recovered more defensive loose balls than his eight. Only one has taken more charges than his four. With Dončić as the primary defender, shooters are converting just 36.7% of their shots against a 45.1 expected FG%; that minus-8.6 is the fourth-largest discrepancy among all players who've contested at least 150 shots.

    According to recent reports, most importantly, the Lakers are 12-2 and tied with the Spurs atop the Western Conference. The Lakers rank as the league's top offense with a rating that balloons to 129.2 points per 100 possessions (which would be an NBA record by a long shot) with Dončić on, and a net rating, as illustrated below, that falls off a cliff when he sits.

    Recent findings suggest that look, if you have Wembanyama ahead of Dončić in the MVP race a month into the season, nobody is going to argue much with you. The oddsmakers slightly favor Wembanyama (+110 at FanDuel; Dončić is +140), who, as you'll see below, has what would qualify as a potentially unanimous case in most years. But this isn't most years. We got a dude averaging nearly 40 points for a No. 1 seed that nobody expected to be a No. 1 seed. Until one of those things changes, it's hard for me to go against Dončić.

    If you think Dončić's plus-35.5 on/off split (it's actually plus-32.2 without filtering for garbage time) is crazy, have a look at Wembanyama's number.

    It has been revealed that victor Wembanyama's impact this season has been another level. Spurs are +42.6 points per 100 possessions with Wemby on the court than off it, according to @cleantheglass. Small sample but other-worldly. Lakers star Luka Dončić is at +35.5 pts/100 poss.Both numbers are better… pic.twitter.com/0GJCFFmZ5K.

    Yes, you're reading that right. The Spurs, for all their supportive talent, fall by 42.6 points per 100 possessions when Wembanyama leaves the court (plus-29.2 on vs. minus-13.3 off), per Cleaning the Glass. By comparison, the best on/off split that Nikola Jokić has ever recorded is plus-24.8. Curry's best is plus-21.3. LeBron James' is plus-17.8. Go down that list and look at the most impactful on-off splits those guys have ever posted. Wembanyama is in another galaxy.

    Recent findings suggest that and it's vital to note that Wembanyama plays on a great team, as all these guys in the graphic have. The fact that there is still so much difference between when Wembanyama is on the court and when he isn't, even in a small sample, is honestly difficult to comprehend. San Antonio's three-guard lineup was supposed to be an experiment, but it's hard to know if Dylan Harper, De'Aaron Fox and Stephon Castle truly optimize one another or if Wembanyama is enough to make any lineup dominant in spite of traditional challenges (like none of those three being a true shooter).

    It has been revealed that wembanyama is the best defensive player on the planet by an immeasurable amount. Even the stats don't do it justice. He's on pace for north of 350 blocks, a number only four players (Elmore Smith, Mark Eaton, Manute Bol and Hakeem Olajuwon) have eclipsed since blocks became an official stat in 1973, and still it's just as much, if not more, about the shots he deters scorers from even attempting.

    In a recent development, and why would they? Scorers are making just 33.6% of their shots when Wembanyama is the nearest defender, a 17% drop from their expected 50.4%. That also leads the league among all players who've defended at least 120 shots, and again, it fails to fully capture his defensive dominance.

    Recent findings suggest that the fact that we've gotten this far without talking about Wembanyama's offense, as if it's a mere afterthought for a guy to be averaging 28.6 points and 11.6 rebounds in under 30 minutes a night. Wembanyama is figuring out his hot spots, prioritizing closer-to-the-basket positioning where he is a skyscraper among regular NBA buildings. He's taking two more paint shots per game than he did last season; 43% of his shots are coming from inside four feet, per Cleaning the Glass, up from 38% last season, and his 4.6 dunks per game (up from 2.7 last year) have him on pace to shatter Rudy Gobert's single-season record of 306.

    If I had to guess, Wembanyama's production is more sustainable than Dončić's. It's hard to imagine Dončić not hitting a rough patch from 3, and he's almost certainly not going to keep scoring 39 points per game. He'll be over 35 points per game when everything is stated and done because that's what the Lakers need from him, but there's a burnout factor while Wembanyama is kind of cruising to these numbers, and the defensive impact is as natural as breathing. My gut notes Wembanyama will be a clearer MVP favorite by Christmas.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey.
    • According to recent reports, kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era.
    • Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

    According to recent reports, kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

    Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

    Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

    Recent findings suggest that it's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

    Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

    Sources indicate that montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

    We already know the Wild are major-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

    Sources indicate that however, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

    With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

    It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

    In a recent development, carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

    Sources indicate that similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

    Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

    Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

    Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.

    Webb, who just recently turned 30, endured a bit of a down 2026 on the run-prevention front, but the overall body of work remains very strong.     #164889. Re-grading the Giannis Antetokounmpo trade: Why the Heat and Bucks both look much worse now

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2333 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cbssports ↗ Open Full Page

    Re-grading the Giannis Antetokounmpo trade: Why the Heat and Bucks both look much worse now

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2333 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that giannis Antetokounmpo will face the Milwaukee Bucks for the first time as an opponent on Wednesday, but it's a game that feels as though it's a half-decade or more in the making.
    • The Bucks kept kicking the can down the road.
    • Now, Antetokounmpo plays for the Heat while the Bucks are in no man's land.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that giannis Antetokounmpo will face the Milwaukee Bucks for the first time as an opponent on Wednesday, but it's a game that feels as though it's a half-decade or more in the making. The Miami Heat were a rumored suitor for Antetokounmpo, who played his first 13 NBA seasons in Milwaukee, as far back as the buildup to his possible 2021 free agency, which the Bucks averted by trading for Jrue Holiday and ultimately winning a championship.

    The Bucks kept kicking the can down the road. They secured another extension with Antetokounmpo in 2023 by trading for Damian Lillard. They stuck their fingers in their ears and pretended everything was fine when Lillard tore his Achilles in 2025, in the process bypassing the chance to trade Antetokounmpo with multiple years left on his contract when they could have maximized his trade value. In the end, though, Heat president Pat Riley did what he has done so many times before: he got his man.

    Now, Antetokounmpo plays for the Heat while the Bucks are in no man's land. We have around four weeks of data on how these teams are going to look after one of the bigger blockbusters in recent NBA history, so with their first head-to-head bout at hand, let's regrade the trade based on everything we now know.

    Let's start with the obvious positive: despite age- and injury-related fears, Antetokounmpo is still mostly himself. He is, by both the counting stats and the all-in-ones, playing either at the level of his Milwaukee peak or somewhere relatively close. He has at the very least been a top 10 player in the NBA this season, and you could argue him into the top five. Miami paid an All-NBA price and has gotten an All-NBA player.

    There are slight signs of slipping in his age-32 season that merit some examination, though they don't come close to triggering any real alarms. His free-throw rate is lower than it's been since 2018, for instance, but it's still near the top of the league. He's scoring 1.38 points per possession when shooting at the rim -- a very good figure that rates him in the 82nd percentile league-wide, per Synergy Sports. We just judge Antetokounmpo on a curve because he was in the 95th percentile last season and generally hovered around the mid-90s when he was winning MVPs and his 2021 championship.

    Sources indicate that this is, again, not a significant concern. He's still great, and he's supplementing his rim finishing with significant improvement from mid-range. After shooting below 39% from mid-range over the past five seasons combined, he's above 51% so far this season. We can say pretty safely at this point that the 3-point shot is never coming for Antetokounmpo, so this shot will be his pathway to both aging gracefully and combating the walls he'll see at the rim in the playoffs. If this is sustainable, it extends his prime another year or two and makes him close to unguardable while he remains near his physical peak. Thus far, last year's calf injuries have not recurred.

    Recent findings suggest that he's slipped defensively. That's almost undeniable. He contested around nine shots per game when he won Defensive Player of the Year in 2020. He's down to around six this season, and opponents are shooting 6% worse within six feet of the basket against Antetokounmpo than they are otherwise, per NBA.com tracking data. That figure was 20.4% in 2020. The all-in-ones share this basic opinion: still good, no longer great. The tape shows an older player who paces himself defensively. He can still summon greatness for stretches, but he's not in the All-Defense mix seriously anymore.

    According to recent reports, that brings us to the bigger picture. When you trade as much as Miami did, the question is never just whether the player is good enough to justify the cost, but whether the team is. Heat fans would point to the team's ongoing 8-2 stretch following its 0-4 start to suggest that it was. Count me as a remaining skeptic.

    Most of those victories came against either the bottom of the league -- the Kings, the Jazz, they needed overtime to beat the Clippers! -- or injured opponents. No Tyrese Haliburton in the Pacers win. No Jalen Duren against the Pistons. No Evan Mobley against the Cavaliers. No Amen Thompson against the Rockets, playing the second night of a back-to-back. They've faced only two true heavy hitters at full strength, the Lakers and Timberwolves, and they stood no chance against either.

    Recent findings suggest that the theory of this team relies on a top-five defense. The offense is simply too reliant on shot creation out of its bigs -- Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo -- to be the leading unit for a champion. The early defensive returns have thus far been discouraging, though in fairness, no team has been unluckier on wide-open opponents' 3s. Even during the 8-2 stretch, they're allowing 48.4 points in the paint per game, a well-below-average figure. Their transition defense is nothing special and they're so-so rebounders. They've hung their hat on turnover-generation, but they're by no means elite on that front. The raw numbers are bad. The truth is closer to fine when you factor in luck. They haven't been great, which is what they need to be.

    In a recent development, part of the problem is that they need to play defensively deficient players -- most notably Klay Thompson and, if he eventually re-earns his rotation spot, Tim Hardaway Jr. -- in order to survive offensively. You can get away with that if everyone else is great. Antetokounmpo has taken a step back. Andrew Wiggins has been a mess. Erik Spoelstra is a defensive miracle worker, but the players here just haven't lived up to expectations. Davion Mitchell has become so important offensively that even he's slipped a bit on that end.

    Mitchell's playmaking has been a godsend, and a pretty surprising one in context. The Heat tried and failed to get the Bucks to take Mitchell instead of Kasparas Jakučionis in the trade. There's no telling how bad things would be without Mitchell at this stage, but we're still talking about a pretty limited scorer who nearly doubled his 3-point volume and free throw attempt rate in a single season. Miami probably can't expect him to carry this sort of burden forever. Pelle Larsson is more of a connector than a creator in his own right. Down the line, another guard who can create off of the dribble is probably needed here, especially without a strong Antetokounmpo-Adebayo two-man game forming thus far.

    Sources indicate that the paths to improvement here are narrow here. The Heat are pressed up against a first-apron hard cap, and they'd need Charlotte's cooperation to amend the protection on their 2027 selection if they wanted to trade even a single first-round pick at this deadline. It's going to take a little while to meaningfully upgrade the supporting talent here, and the rest of the Heat offseason reflected that.

    According to recent reports, they could have perhaps generated the cap flexibility to retain Norman Powell. They elected instead to let him walk, and when they extended Wiggins, they chose to front-load the deal by using his player option rather than spreading the money out to create more immediate hard cap room. Rather than signing a mid-level free agent to a multi-year deal, they added the older Hardaway on just a one-year contract, presumably to maintain optionality going into next summer.

    If Antetokounmpo were 28, this patience might make sense. He turns 32 in less than a month. The time to go all-in around him is now. It's an ironic middle ground that the Heat have put themselves in. Miami could justify the cost it paid for Antetokounmpo only through immediate contention, yet they're slow-playing the roster build in what you would expect, just based on the standard aging curve, to be the best individual season left in his career. It really doesn't make sense to do this halfway.

    Recent findings suggest that we're talking about the Heat here. They've made the Finals with less talent than they have now, and they are organizationally opposed to intentional rebuilds. There was never a conversation here about, say, trading Adebayo and starting over as opposed to pushing chips in for someone like Antetokounmpo. But if a few years pass and the Heat don't at least make the conference finals with this core, it's going to be worth wondering if that's the path they should have taken. The early returns here are mixed. The Heat bet their future on a single player. He may be good enough to warrant that investment, but the jury's still out on whether their team actually is.

    Sources indicate that the Bucks dug themselves an enormous hole by refusing to trade Antetokounmpo when the whole world knew they should have. It was over the moment Lillard tore his Achilles. At that point, Antetokounmpo had two years left on his contract, so hypothetical rental trades would have been feasible. He was younger and he hadn't yet lost a year to calf injuries, so his value was higher. Asset-rich teams like the Spurs and Rockets might have been interested. Had the Bucks moved Antetokounmpo in 2025, they would have gotten substantially more than they wound up getting. Instead, they made the disastrous decision not only to keep him but also to waive and stretch Lillard to sign Myles Turner. Yikes.

    When the Bucks finally realized they'd reached the point of no return, Antetokounmpo, as an expiring contract, had complete control of the situation. At least four teams with strong offers were turned away because Antetokounmpo simply wasn't interested in extending with them, according to ESPN. He only wanted the Heat or Celtics. Given those circumstances, the Bucks still managed the negotiations as well as they reasonably could have. They used the Celtics as an effective scare tactic to compel Miami to give up pretty much all of its available draft capital, plus Jakučionis instead of Mitchell.

    Industry observers note that you can win a negotiation and still lose a trade, though, when most of the things the other team had to give in a trade just weren't that valuable. The major swing piece here was Kel'El Ware, an extremely high-risk, high-reward young big man with star-level raw talent and a pretty iffy reputation when it comes to his motor and commitment. The Bucks, thus far, have gotten the worst version of him. He's playing less in his third season with the Bucks than he did in two years with the Heat despite being on the worst roster of his career. He's missing shots everywhere, his defense has been miserable, and if he's ever going to reach that sky-high ceiling, it's probably going to have to come on his third team.

    That, in a nutshell, is the problem here. The Bucks traded the greatest player in franchise history, one of the 25 or so best players the league has ever seen, and got no one who could credibly be considered a cornerstone moving forward. Ware looks like a swing and a miss. It's too early to say much on Nate Ament, but he's a No. 13 overall draft pick, so odds are, he's going to be fine and not much better. Tyler Herro and Jaime Jaquez Jr. are both about what they expected, but both will need to be paid next summer. Herro's presence exacerbates a preexisting glut of guards. His presence has forced last year's breakout guard, Ryan Rollins, to the bench. Maybe that makes him a bit cheaper as a free agent next summer. It also probably sours him on a future in Milwaukee.

    Industry observers note that speaking of the guard glut, the Gary Trent Jr. investigation looms large over this trade. The NBA set a notable precedent in the Kawhi Leonard case that it is willing to strip teams of draft picks acquired through trade. This is notable because the Bucks have so little control over their own first-round picks moving forward. The picks they got from the Heat in 2031 and 2033, at least for now, are the crown jewels of this trade. Both of them are theoretically vulnerable if the NBA finds that the Bucks circumvented the salary cap.

    It's even worth wondering if the Bucks should or could have used the Antetokounmpo situation as an escape hatch on any preexisting agreements with Trent, if one actually existed. If the Bucks felt an obligation to pay Trent more than the market suggested he was worth, and if they knew they had so many guards that he was unlikely to factor into their rotation (he played less than 40 total minutes before bizarrely leading the Bucks in playing time in Sunday's loss to the Hawks despite coming off the bench), then why not use the leverage Antetokounmpo's availability granted them to foist Trent on Miami through a sign-and-trade? Of course, if the Bucks had the foresight to do this, they probably wouldn't be in this situation in the first place. For now, the investigation is ongoing and we know little beyond the sheer ridiculousness of the contract itself.

    Sources indicate that the Bucks are 1-13 as of this writing. That, roughly, was to be expected. This was a bad team with Antetokounmpo, so inevitably, removing an MVP candidate was going to make it far worse. But to leave a trade involving a player of that caliber without a single blue-chip player or draft pick is frankly embarrassing.

    Sources indicate that the Bucks bungled this Antetokounmpo saga for a year, and even if they managed its end stages properly, they'd dug themselves so deep a hole that there was just no obvious way out of it. Now, it seems they may well have made the situation worse with Trent after the fact. This was an organization-wide debacle.

    • Which teams might make for a good fit for Webb?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Coming off a disaster of a season and with a roster badly in need of an overhaul, the Giants make sense as a team to make a trade or two this offseason. Sure enough, they are "listening to trade offers" for All-Star starting pitcher Logan Webb, per The Athletic, but they'd need a "very strong return" in order to deal him.

    According to recent reports, webb, 30, has two years and $47 million left on his current deal. He went 8-9 with a 4.31 ERA and 1.3 WAR last season, but it was his worst year in quite a while. He averaged 4.5 WAR per season in the previous four years with a 3.22 ERA and led the National League in innings pitched from 2023 to 2025, racking up three straight top-six Cy Young finishes.

    Which teams might make for a good fit for Webb? Many of them. We're talking about a workhorse under team control for two more years. Let's run through five of the best fits while, again, knowing that basically any contender should be interested in at least a conversation with the Giants.

    Sources indicate that the Cubs need so much pitching this offseason. Their entire rotation heading into the playoffs last season is in free agency. This isn't hyperbole. Matthew Boyd, Shota Imanaga, Kevin Gausman, Clay Holmes and David Peterson are all off the roster. If the Cubs were to try and put together a rotation right now, it would be something like Justin Steele, Edward Cabrera, Javier Assad and several question marks. Ben Brown and Cade Horton will open the season on the injured list.

    Do we really need to spell out what a reliable innings eater would mean for this bunch? Webb is an outstanding fit here.

    The upstart playoff team last season was a ton of fun, but also was running bullpen games in the ALDS. The White Sox just attached Davis Martin to Luis Castillo in a trade to the Rockies in order to offload Castillo's contract, too, so they're down a starter. The Dustin May signing means they have him along with Sean Burke and converted reliever Grant Taylor. The White Sox would reportedly like to sign another starter in the May ballpark, but what about trading for someone better like Webb?

    A top four in the rotation of Webb, Burke, Taylor and May would be exponentially better than what the Sox had last season.

    Returns of Spencer Strider and Spencer Schwellenbach at some point will help, but this is still a thin rotation for a team coming off a division title. Chris Sale remains, but he's followed up with Grant Holmes and Bryce Elder before the Spencers return. Youngster Didier Fuentes moving to the rotation is exciting, but there are an awful lot of questions behind Sale, who turns 38 in late March, by the way.

    It has been revealed that given that the Padres reside in the NL West with the Giants, there might be a bit of an intradivision tax in terms of the asking price, but Padres boss A.J. Preller is never shy about offloading prospects. There could certainly be a fit. The Padres need rotation help, too, after losing Michael King, Nick Pivetta, Robbie Ray and others to free agency. We know they're in on Tarik Skubal, but that doesn't mean they'll be content with just landing one significant fish.

    Look at the current Padres rotation. It's basically Joe Musgrove and Randy Vásquez. With three straight playoff berths and zero trips to the World Series, now isn't the time to have Jhony Brito, Ryan Weiss and Ian Koenig make up 60% of the rotation.

    Dealing for Webb and signing Skubal would make for a nice offseason for fresh ownership, no?

    One of the most disappointing teams in baseball last season needs to have a prolific offseason. We've heard plenty about the Mets being involved in the Skubal sweepstakes and we've seen them win a monster bidding war before (see: Soto, Juan). Grabbing Webb would make it quite a well-rounded rotation with talented youngsters Nolan McLean, Christian Scott and Zac Thornton.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Justin Herbert is in the NFL's concussion protocol after the Chargers' 27-24 loss to the Jets, per the team. It's unclear when Herbert suffered the injury, as he played the whole game, but concussion-like symptoms can appear well after the collisions that cause the concussions themselves.

    Because he entered concussion protocol, Herbert did not address the media after the game.

    In a recent development, herbert went 15-for-21 for 131 yards and two touchdowns and ran for 32 yards and a score as well. He took six sacks, though, and has now taken an NFL-high 39 sacks this season.

    Herbert has been an ironman, especially considering the hits he has taken in his career behind a seemingly ever-shaky offensive line. Only one injury has forced Herbert to miss a game in his career: A fractured finger on his throwing hand required surgery and cost him the final four contests of the 2023 campaign.

    The Chargers (1-9) have had a miserable season, with the much-hyped pairing of Herbert and offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel failing to mesh. Herbert has thrown just eight touchdown passes compared to 11 interceptions and is on pace for career worsts nearly across the board. He had played his first two turnover-free games of the season — last week in a win over the Ravens and Sunday against New York — but now could miss time depending on how concussion protocol progresses.

    Sources indicate that if entering the protocol does force Herbert to miss time, the Chargers would turn to DJ Uiagalelei. He has played in one NFL game, in mop-up duty against the Texans in Week 9. He went 2-for-7 for 24 yards and a touchdown. Los Angeles also has Jake Browning on the practice squad.

    Industry observers note that welcome to Thanksgiving week. Here in Major League Baseball news, that normally means we're bound for a slow week -- save for a few notable exceptions -- but with the CBA expiring on Dec. 1, we might just be in for a free agent frenzy. Let's hope that's the case.

    We can start today's set of news and rumors with the biggest free agent out there.

    Tarik Skubal is the No. 1 free agent this offseason and the two-time Cy Young winner appears on pace to make a decision before the CBA expires. Skubal's agent, Scott Boras, hit MLB Network Radio on Sunday and mentioned that there's a "strong likelihood" that a decision comes by that Dec. 1 deadline, especially given that Skubal's signing impacts so many other pitchers (Boras mentioned that it impacts "10-15 pitchers").

    The 30-year-old lefty was 12-7 with a 2.72 ERA and 186 strikeouts in 158 ⅔ innings last season, as he bounced back after just six weeks from elbow surgery.

    The teams most heavily involved in the Skubal rumors to this point have been the Dodgers, Mets, Padres and Blue Jays, all of whom had in-person meetings with him last week.

    The Tigers have agreed to a deal with right-hander Luis Gil, per ESPN. It's a one-year, $2.3 million deal.

    Gil won the American League Rookie of the Year after a productive 2024 season in which he won 15 games and had a 3.50 ERA, but he spent a good portion of 2026 in the minors and was nontendered by the Yankees on Friday. In his limited MLB time last season, Gil had a 4.61 ERA, 1.43 WHIP and 17 strikeouts in 27 ⅓ innings.

    The Tigers rotation seems set with Framber Valdez, Troy Melton, Keider Montero, Jackson Jobe and River Ryan, so consider Gil a depth option.

    NFL Week 11 winners and losers: Cowboys offense makes history in get-right win, Steelers slump

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1773 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Dallas Cowboys have to light up the scoreboard to win games in 2026, and they did just that in Week 11.
    • Dallas, therefore, is among the biggest winners of the week across the NFL this week.
    • But at the same time, the Pittsburgh Steelers were among the teams to feel the sting of failing to live up to expectations against a beleaguered opponent.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Dallas Cowboys have to light up the scoreboard to win games in 2026, and they did just that in Week 11. The superstars on their offense showed up emphatically in a "gotta have it" kind of game against the Tennessee Titans and, for at least one week, deflected some of the deserved scrutiny that has been trained on the defense all season.

    Dallas, therefore, is among the biggest winners of the week across the NFL this week. Sunday's schedule was one where heavy favorites had little to gain but everything to lose, and to the Cowboys' credit, they not only avoided disaster but also took care of business in emphatic fashion. They were not the only team to do so, but they needed that kind of win more than any of the other franchises that entered the week on the right side of a lopsided point spread.

    But at the same time, the Pittsburgh Steelers were among the teams to feel the sting of failing to live up to expectations against a beleaguered opponent.

    Here are the greatest winners and losers from Sunday's Week 11 action.

    Industry observers note that the defense is still an glitch even after Christian Parker's demotion from play-caller, as evidenced by the 30 points it surrendered to the lowly Titans and the breakdown that allowed Carnell Tate to score one of the strangest touchdowns of the year. But when a team can score at will, what happens on the other side of the ball hardly matters. That was the case for the Cowboys in a 51-30 drubbing of the Titans.

    Dallas needed a win in this spot, and they got it in the worst way. A season that is already slipping through its fingers would have only gotten more depressing with a loss to a one-win team. Behind a nearly perfect game from Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens, Javonte Williams and the rest of the offense, the Cowboys avoided disaster by a healthy margin and notched their third win in five games, keeping them very much alive in the NFC East race.

    It has been revealed that the Cowboys scored on all of their possessions except the final one when they knelt out the clock. They found the end zone seven times and scored a touchdown on each of their first six drives, the franchise's longest run of consecutive possessions ending in a touchdown to open a game in the play-by-play era. Some of that success had to do with the Titans' bleak defensive situation—their 13 straight drives with points allowed dating back to Week 10 were the most in a single season since at least 2000, per NFL research—but just as much with the star power on their own offense.

    In the process, Lamb became the first receiver in Cowboys history with six consecutive 1,000-yard seasons. He and Pickens both crossed the 100-yard mark in the blowout.

    The last time the Steelers beat the Philadelphia Eagles in the City of Brotherly Love? 1965. Granted, as members of opposite conferences, the in-state rivals only play every few years. But this is a losing streak that now spans 12 games after Sunday's 19-16 result, which went in favor of the Eagles.

    It has been revealed that this was the kind of matchup that was supposed to help the Steelers bounce back from last week's no-show against the Cincinnati Bengals and work their way back toward the top of the AFC North. Instead, they lost to a team that hadn't won a game since September and started Joe Milton at quarterback. It is far too early to call it a devastating loss, but if the Steelers finish the season a game short of a playoff berth, it is a contest they will look back on as one they should have gotten.

    The Carolina Panthers survived a shootout with the Baltimore Ravens that stands competitively among the most entertaining and chaotic games of the season. There were seven lead changes in the contest, including four in a back-and-forth second quarter and two in the final period. The Panthers were responsible for that final go-ahead play: A 37-yard field goal from Ryan Fitzgerald with 1:44 to play. The kick put the NFC South leaders up 35-33.

    On a day when every other team in the division either lost or was on a bye, the Panthers capitalized on their opportunity to distance themselves from the pack. They now stand two games clear of the three other squads, all with 3-7 records.

    Sources indicate that A loss would not have cost Carolina its division lead, but it would have been a difficult pill to swallow, given the Ravens hadn't even led in a game since Oct. 25, before the multiple advantages they held on Sunday. But by taking care of business at home against the reeling Ravens, Carolina improved to .500 on the year and is now looking like a more respectable division leader.

    High yardage total aside, Trevor Lawrence had a day to forget. His 301 passing yards were more a product of the large passing volume required of him in a loss than anything else. The New York Giants defense had him pressing in a 23-18 loss and forced him into a number of errors including two interceptions, a pick on a 2-point attempt, three sacks and a whopping 22 incompletions.

    Recent findings suggest that rarely have the Jacksonville Jaguars found themselves in negative game scripts this season. Lawrence was fantastic in one of them (when he threw four touchdowns in a loss to the Houston Texans) but struggled in two others.

    It took until the fourth quarter for Lawrence to lead the Jaguars to a touchdown, but by that point, it was too late. The Giants had already done enough damage in building a 14-point lead. Jacksonville needed Lawrence's typical MVP-caliber passing ability to shine in order to pull off the comeback but did not get it. And as a result, they are behind pace in the battle for the No. 1 seed in the AFC.

    This deep into such a lengthy and legendary career, Travis Kelce routinely reaches landmarks on team and league leaderboards. Sunday was another historic day for the Kansas City Chiefs tight end. Kelce scored two touchdowns in the 34-7 rout of the Arizona Cardinals and thus hauled in multiple scoring passes for the first time in 47 games. Ending that prolonged drought also moved Kelce up a spot on the NFL tight end career touchdown list.

    What better day to make history than the same day on which Kelce became the fourth player in Chiefs history to play 100 regular-season games at Arrowhead Stadium? That is some serious longevity.

    In a recent development, as if the loss to the Eagles was not bad enough for DK Metcalf and the Steelers, the wide receiver made his day even worse with an inexcusable decision. Metcalf had been jawing at Philadelphia defenders all game and took it to another level when he poked Cooper DeJean in the eye a little more than halfway through the third quarter. That exchange drew an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty (Metcalf's second of the game) and prompted his ejection from the game.

    DK Metcalf has been ejected in PhillyCBS | Paramount+ pic.twitter.com/johlxzOD1J.

    Industry observers note that metcalf did not back up his trash talk with his performance. He caught just one pass for 2 yards across four targets.

    The NFL fined Metcalf earlier this season for taunting in the Steelers' Week 4 loss to the Browns. He also served a two-game suspension last season for getting into a physical altercation with a fan.

    Recent findings suggest that the Chicago Bears' trade deadline blockbuster continues to age to perfection. Jeffery Simmons has been nothing but a superstar since his arrival in the Windy City and turned in his best performance as a Bear in the 21-13 win over the Fresh Orleans Saints. Simmons racked up three sacks for the second time in his career, also recording three tackles for loss in a game for the fourth time. He led a vicious pass rush that got home on Tyler Shough six times.

    In a recent development, each of general manager Ryan Poles' moves ahead of and during the season contributed to where the Bears stand as a contender for the NFC's No. 1 seed. The Simmons trade is the latest and most stupendous example, but Poles made several other transactions that have been just as impactful. The Garrett Bradbury trade added a reliable starter to the middle of the offensive line, and sending DJ Moore out of town for two draft picks opened the door for Luther Burden III and Rome Odunze to flourish as a prolific receiving tandem.

    It has been revealed that it is a good thing for the Los Angeles Chargers that they finally ended their winless season last week, because if Sunday's showing is any indication of what is to come over the final month of the season, one win is all they might end up with. A home game against the reeling Newly introduced York Jets is about as winnable of an opportunity as there is in the NFL in 2026, but the Chargers could not take advantage. They dropped to 1-9 on the year with the 27-24 loss.

    Industry observers note that making matters worse, Justin Herbert is now in concussion protocol. DJ Uiagalelei is the No. 2 quarterback and has never started a game.

    Recent findings suggest that this was a chance for Los Angeles to begin stacking wins and make this disaster of a season look a little less devastating. There is some runway ahead with games against the Drake Maye-less Fresh England Patriots, the sub-.500 Tampa Bay Buccaneers and a Las Vegas Raiders team starting a rookie quarterback. Had the Chargers gotten the job done against the Jets, they could have legitimately sparked a hot streak. But following the loss and with Herbert's status in question, they might just slip deeper into a hole.

    Entering Sunday, the last time home teams went undefeated in the early window was back in Week 9 of the 2019 season. It was therefore a rare sight to see the Panthers, Eagles, Chiefs, Cowboys, Bears, Detroit Lions and Buffalo Bills all defend home turf during the 1 p.m. ET slate.

    Including the Texans on "Thursday Night Football," home teams opened the week at 8-0.

    The Broncos and Giants added to the ledger in the late window, while the Chargers were the only home squad to fall. The final tally heading into the Sunday night game was 10-1.

    NBA Power Rankings: The LaMelo Ball effect is being felt in two places; Lakers take top spot from Spurs

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (779 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When Timberwolves star Anthony Edwards went down after four games, I ranked it as the biggest injury blow any team has suffered this season, which was saying a lot given all the injuries we've seen.
    • Sources indicate that how are they doing it?
    • And by elite, we mean the best in the league.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When Timberwolves star Anthony Edwards went down after four games, I ranked it as the biggest injury blow any team has suffered this season, which was saying a lot given all the injuries we've seen. As it turned out, Oklahoma City's barrage of injuries, Kawhi Leonard in Toronto, Tyrese Haliburton in Indiana, Jaren Jackson Jr. in Utah, Paolo Banchero in Orlando, and now Stephen Curry with the Warriors have all turned out to be significantly more debilitating as Minnesota has gone 8-3 without Edwards.

    Sources indicate that how are they doing it? Let's take a look.

    And by elite, we mean the best in the league. Minnesota is surrendering just 104 points per 100 possessions. Give Rudy Gobert his flowers, man. The Wolves' defensive rating drops to 97 points per 100 when he's on the court, while rising to 108.6 when he sits. That stated, the Wolves have defenders everywhere you look and they are seriously tied together.

    With their four regular starters on the floor (LaMelo Ball, Jaden McDaniels, Jonathan Kuminga and Gobert), Minnesota is registering a 92.0 defensive rating with a plus-20.5 net rating. But even when they go smaller and swap in Ayo Dosunmu for Gobert with the other three, the rating stays at 94.2 with a plus-16.2 net.

    No matter the combination, if four of those five guys are on the court, the defense is no worse than 96.0. It's super impressive stuff, and so much for the idea that Ball is a defensive liability. Speaking of Ball ...

    Sources indicate that the LaMelo effect is being felt in two places: Minnesota, of course, but also Charlotte, where the offense has plummeted from a 123.3 rating with Ball on the court last year to a league-worst 103.1 this season. Being down Kon Knueppel doesn't help, but it's night and day watching this unit try to generate clean looks without Ball's creation and passing.

    Meanwhile, the Wolves are flying. The defense is carrying the day and we're going to get to some of the guys carrying more impressive statistical weight than Ball, at least relatively, but watch this team play and try to argue his impact isn't all over the floor. He won the game for Minnesota on Tuesday with two defensive plays over the closing seconds.

    LaMelo wins the game with back to back defensive plays! Who would have thought? 👀 pic.twitter.com/v9xYpR7eZu.

    Industry observers note that of course, his impact is felt most offensively. The pace. Energy. All of Minnesota's shooting percentages go up with Ball on the court, as they did last season in Charlotte, and that's not because of Ball's own shooting. He's only making 41.8% of his own shots, after all. It's his passing, his flow. As fancy as it is, it's fundamental in its contagious, force-multiplying impact.

    Industry observers note that the bottom line is this: Over his last 53 games between Charlotte and Minnesota, Ball has gone 39-14. That's the pace of a 60-win team. He's an agent of chaos, fine. It can look out of control. He still chucks up the playground shots, often off one foot and from barely inside the boundary. But we all wondered what it would look like when he was playing for a team with real stakes. Is he a winner? Or are his stats empty? Honestly, he's not even that impressive of a stats guy so far. He's just a winner.

    The Wolves can deploy uncompromised lineups up and down their roster, meaning they don't have to decide between offense and defense. All their guys do both. They also have multiple offensive weapons even without Edwards, which is why Ball isn't having to carry a bigger scoring burden than he's equipped to handle, at least efficiently.

    In a recent development, terrence Shannon Jr. put up 34 off the bench in a win over Portland on Monday. The next night, Dosunmu and McDaniels, who are playing at legit All-Star levels, combined for 52 with nine 3-pointers. Kuminga is giving them 12.8 points, 5.7 rebounds, almost three assists and a steal over 30 minutes per game.

    Other than Gobert, Jaylen Clark is really the only truly offensively limited guy, but for the minutes he gets, he is one hell of a defender. You do not want this man guarding you. You do not want anything to do with this team overall.

    It has been revealed that they came out of the gate looking incredible with Edwards and Ball looking like basketball brothers. It seemed like that was going to die out when Edwards got hurt. It hasn't.

    When Edwards gets back, this Timberwolves team has the look of a legitimate contender.

    Breaking: Paul George embracing role as second option to Jayson Tatum: 'Not one of those guys that have to have an ego'

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (847 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that the entire basketball world has spent the past five months or so trying to figure out what exactly caused the beef, or, well, lamb chops and gravy, between Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown.
    • We know the Celtics tried to trade Brown for Giannis Antetokounmpo.
    • In a recent development, regardless, there are clearly some hard feelings here.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that the entire basketball world has spent the past five months or so trying to figure out what exactly caused the beef, or, well, lamb chops and gravy, between Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown. The two coexisted harmoniously as teammates on the Boston Celtics for the better part of a decade. They won a championship together and reached the Eastern Conference Finals five times. That run ended this summer with Boston's stunning decision to swap Brown for Paul George and draft picks, and we've never quite gotten to the bottom of what's happened since.

    We know the Celtics tried to trade Brown for Giannis Antetokounmpo. After moving Brown to the Philadelphia 76ers, Brad Stevens spoke about the team's need to both spread its financial resources and its usage among a wider group of players. Celtics broadcaster Brian Scalabrine claimed that Brown went to the organization with a list of demands that, if not met, would be followed by a trade request. Brown's camp has denied this claim, and Scalabrine himself has walked it back. Marc Spears reported in July that he had heard Brown felt like the Celtics treated Tatum as though he was the organizational favorite.

    In a recent development, regardless, there are clearly some hard feelings here. Brown claimed last offseason that the 2025-26 season was his personal favorite as a professional. Tatum missed most of that season, and Brown had his best statistical season. Brown claimed early this season that Tatum has a "hell of a PR team," and then he snubbed him at tip-off before their first game as opponents, a Celtics victory. That game was owned by George, Brown's replacement in Boston.

    So far, the partnership has been harmonious. George is outplaying Brown thus far this season. He's been among the NBA's very best 3-point shooters, has spearheaded a system shift in Boston's defense that has finally allowed the Celtics to generate some turnovers, and he's done so on fewer shot attempts per game (15.7) than Brown has taken in any season since the 2019-20 campaign. Boston's vision for the George fit has proven accurate, and that's been as true in the press as it has been on the court.

    George addressed his partnership with Tatum in an interview with The Athletic on Wednesday, and he made it clear that his role is to "help JT," in clear deference to Boston's remaining superstar. "I'm just not one of those guys that have to have an ego," George said. "My ego comes from what I do on the court when the ball gets thrown up and how I impact the game and how I affect the game in all aspects. My ego doesn't have to come from me stroking it or me thinking I'm bigger than someone or better than someone.

    In a recent development, "But with that is, I know where I'm at in my career. I'm at the end of my career. Tatum, JT has (many) more years ahead of him, and he's someone that I admired from afar. And to see where he's taken his game, how much better he's gotten and him having all the tools and weapons to be the best player in the league, how can I help that? How can I support that and get him there?".

    It has been revealed that george and Brown are fundamentally different players. Brown, younger and a better scorer off the dribble, was well-suited to lifting last year's Celtics to a surprising 56-win season despite their shorthanded roster. But George's superior shooting and low-maintenance playing style have suited Tatum perfectly, and the fact that he's at a point in his career in which he's eager to take a backseat to Tatum helps with whatever palace intrigue occurred between Tatum and Brown at the end of their joint run.

    If Brown was indeed frustrated with the idea of playing second fiddle to Tatum, it hasn't shown in Philadelphia. His 76ers are 12-3, he's openly called them Tyrese Maxey's team, and he played a key role in recruiting LeBron James, another ball-dominant star, to join the team in free agency. His usage on this star-studded 76ers roster is at its lowest rate since the 2019-20 season. Clearly, this was not as simple as Brown wanting his own team as so many suggested.

    But something created a rift in Boston that led to where we are now, and so far, everyone involved should be happy with how this has played out. The 76ers and Celtics have the two best records in the Eastern Conference. George is playing better in Boston than he ever did in Philadelphia. Tatum is playing better with George than he ever did with Brown. And Brown has become an essential component of a different contender rather than being forced to start from scratch on a bad team as he would have if he'd been traded to the Milwaukee Bucks for Antetokounmpo.

    On the court, at least, egos haven't been a problem for anybody, and the deal is working out for everyone.

Nonostante alcuni infortuni, i capitolini mettono in campo una prestazione brillante e conquistano i tre punti con autorità. Il primo tempo è stato ottimo e non siamo riusciti a concretizzare delle situazioni. Dopo il 2-0 la gara si è messa in salita.     💡 Key Takeaways
    • Boston Celtics coach Joe Mazzulla called on star forward Jayson Tatum to be "better" after he was called for a controversial technical foul in the closing seconds of Wednesday's 105-101 loss, which effectively sealed the game for the Denver Nuggets.
    • "We can't put ourselves in that position to even give the refs an opportunity to interpret it a certain type of way," Mazzulla remarked after the game.
    • With 6.4 seconds remaining, Jamal Murray worked off a huge screen from Nikola Jokić, created space with a nasty step-back on Neemias Queta and buried a difficult jumper to give the Nuggets a three-point lead.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Boston Celtics coach Joe Mazzulla called on star forward Jayson Tatum to be "better" after he was called for a controversial technical foul in the closing seconds of Wednesday's 105-101 loss, which effectively sealed the game for the Denver Nuggets.

    "We can't put ourselves in that position to even give the refs an opportunity to interpret it a certain type of way," Mazzulla remarked after the game. "Gotta be better.".

    With 6.4 seconds remaining, Jamal Murray worked off a huge screen from Nikola Jokić, created space with a nasty step-back on Neemias Queta and buried a difficult jumper to give the Nuggets a three-point lead. The Celtics, who had led by as many as 17 late in the first half, still had a chance to tie, however. At least, they did, until Tatum threw the ball toward referee John Goble.

    According to recent reports, the baseline official, Eric Dalen, immediately hit Tatum with a technical foul. Murray stepped to the line and made the free throw to put the Nuggets up by four.

    Sources indicate that "I told [Dalen], like, I wasn't mad. Wasn't a foul on me; we just called a timeout," Tatum said. "John Goble called a timeout and pointed at our bench. Thought he was looking this way, but yeah, he called a tech. For me, just find the female ref that was there, or the other ref, and whoever was probably closest, I should have just gave them the ball.".

    Jamal Murray hits a clutch jumper to extend the Nuggets the lead to 3, with 6.4 seconds remaining in regulation.The Celtics call a timeout, and Jayson Tatum throws the ball towards the ref John Goble, who wasn't looking, and receives a technical foul, which Murray converts to… pic.twitter.com/PZtzl0zs3D.

    Tatum's controversial technical capped a brutal second half for the Celtics and their star.

    Recent findings suggest that after scoring 20 points in the first half to help the Celtics build a 17-point lead, Tatum managed just four points in the second half on 2-of-6 shooting with five turnovers. Notably, he missed mid-range attempts on back-to-back possessions in the final two minutes. The first could have pushed the Celtics' lead back up to three, while the latter would have put them in front.

    According to recent reports, "The four turnovers I had in the third quarter really put us out of sync," Tatum noted. "In those situations, I gotta communicate better, I gotta execute better, I gotta take care of the ball. I think that kinda put us in a hole, and was the turning point for the game.".

    This defeat was the first time all season that the Celtics have lost back-to-back games. Now 11-4, the Celtics are 1 ½ games back of the Philadelphia 76ers for the No. 1 seed in the Eastern Conference. Come April, when seeding battles are heating up, the Celtics may rue this one.

    In the second half, as their lead melted away, the Celtics turned the ball over 11 times, were called for 20 fouls (which led to 22 Nuggets free throws) and shot 2 of 19 from 3-point range. Two of the Celtics' four defeats this season have now involved a major blown lead: 22 points against the Detroit Pistons on opening day and 17 points against the Nuggets.

    Tarik Skubal signing with Mets: Two-time Cy Young winner lands historic nine-year, $450 million contract

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (726 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ace left-hander Tarik Skubal, winner of the last two American League Cy Young awards and far and away the top free agent of the 2026-27 class, has agreed to terms with the Fresh York Mets on a nine-year contract worth $450 million, reports the New York Post.
    • Once finalized, the deal will make Skubal the highest-paid pitcher in Major League Baseball history, in terms of both total contract value and average annual salary.
    • Skubal, who turned 30 years of age on Nov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ace left-hander Tarik Skubal, winner of the last two American League Cy Young awards and far and away the top free agent of the 2026-27 class, has agreed to terms with the Fresh York Mets on a nine-year contract worth $450 million, reports the New York Post. The deal has a $45 million signing bonus with no options or opt-outs, per SNY, as well as a full no-trade clause, so the Mets have locked Skubal up for the full nine years. Further, there are only $30 million in deferrals, according to the New York Post. The deal is pending a physical.

    Once finalized, the deal will make Skubal the highest-paid pitcher in Major League Baseball history, in terms of both total contract value and average annual salary.

    Skubal, who turned 30 years of age on Nov. 20, is the No. 1 ranked talent on our list of the top 50 free agents for this offseason. Here's part of Mike Axisa's write-up:.

    "Excluding Yoshinobu Yamamoto, who was a special case as a Japanese star with no MLB track record, Skubal is the best starting pitcher to hit free agency since Gerrit Cole in 2019. He revealed few long-lasting effects from the NanoScope elbow surgery in May and remains a capital-A Ace with terrific surface stats and under-the-hood performance indicators. Skubal brings four swing-and-miss pitches to the table (four-seamer, changeup, slider, curveball), a near MLB-best ability to limit exit velocity, and elite strike-throwing ability (MLB's third-lowest walk rate since 2023). Build an ace starter in a lab and he would look a lot like Skubal. He'll play the entire 2027 season at age 30, and given the things teams can do with pitchers these days, Skubal figures to remain a frontline starter for most of a long-term contract. He's the only true balance-of-power player available in free agency this offseason. Skubal can swing a division race and a postseason series all by himself.".

    Sources indicate that over the last three seasons, Skubal has pitched to a 2.42 ERA and an FIP of 2.48 in 546 innings spread over 88 starts. That amounts to a total WAR of 17.7 since the start of the 2024 campaign. Skubal remains foremost in the discussion for best pitcher in baseball, and this signing reflects that reality.

    Since Skubal was traded to the Los Angeles Dodgers from the Detroit Tigers leading up to the 2026 deadline, he was ineligible to receive the qualifying offer from the Dodgers. As such, the Mets will not be penalized a draft pick for signing Skubal.

    In a recent development, the nine years here aren't record-setting, as the longest pitcher contract remains the 12-year deal that Yoshinobu Yamamoto signed with the Dodgers. Yamamoto's $325 million was previously the largest contract for a pitcher -- obviously excepting Shohei Ohtani, as he's a two-way player -- so Skubal's $450 million shatters that record.

    In a recent development, coming off a disappointing 88-loss campaign in 2026, the Mets, big-spending owner Steve Cohen, and lead decision-maker David Stearns needed to make an offseason splash to improve their chances of a 2027 rebound and inspire a perhaps disaffected fan base. Skubal more than qualifies. He'll front a Mets rotation that also includes 25-year-old right-hander Nolan McLean, who himself has frontline long-term potential. In Queens, Skubal joins a roster that also includes the All-Star likes of Juan Soto, Francisco Lindor, and Bo Bichette.

    Further, the Mets just locked up young outfielder A.J. Ewing to an eight-year, $95 million extension and we all know plenty about Soto's monster contract. The Mets now have Soto through 2039, Skubal through 2035, Ewing through 2034 and Lindor through 2031.

    The rotation for the Mets right now looks something like:.

    Given the large outlay for Skubal here, the Mets should be all-in on improving the ballclub for the 2027 season, which means we shouldn't expect them to stop with just signing Skubal. That last spot in the rotation, as such, should be ticketed to someone else outside the organization at present, whether a free agent or a trade acquisition.

    The landing of the top free agent available no doubt ramps up the pressure on Stearns and the Mets to deliver a playoff berth and a deep October run in 2027, but Skubal's presence also makes it much likely that such a feat comes to pass.
